Why this project matters

Parking violations and reported collisions offer two different views of how Vancouver streets are used. Bringing them together helps reveal recurring enforcement hotspots, changing road-level patterns and locations worth investigating for safety improvements. The dashboard is an exploratory planning tool—not a definitive measure of crash risk or street-design quality.

Who can use it?

Municipal transportation planners, road-safety analysts, public policy researchers, enforcement teams and community advocates can use these views to identify questions for further study and prioritize field investigations.

Questions worth investigating

  • Which roads show persistent parking-ticket concentration, and how does that change by year or infraction type?
  • Where do ticket hotspots and approximate collision hotspots overlap—or diverge?
  • Could intersection geometry, curbside loading, sightlines, crossings, turning movements or parking restrictions help explain patterns at selected sites?
  • Which candidate locations warrant site visits, traffic-volume measurements and before/after evaluation of street-design changes?

Research boundary: Spatial overlap is a hypothesis generator, not evidence that parking violations cause collisions or that road design is responsible. Any intervention should be evaluated using traffic and pedestrian exposure, observed street conditions, collision severity, engineering standards and community feedback.

Project architecture

The five-stage architecture connects official source datasets to standardized and geographically matched records, road-level metrics, an interactive map and reusable portfolio deliverables. Quality checks and documented uncertainty are part of the pipeline—not afterthoughts.

Technical workflow

The detailed pipeline shows street-name standardization, block and road matching, collision-location interpretation, data-quality auditing, comparative road-level analysis and interactive visualization. It illustrates how raw municipal records become research-ready geographic summaries.

Project overview

An end-to-end geospatial analytics project connecting City of Vancouver parking violations (2020–2025), the municipal road network, and ICBC collision data (2021–2025). The workflow standardizes source records, performs approximate geographic matching, audits data quality, and presents road-level patterns through a published interactive dashboard.

Research question

How do parking enforcement patterns, changes across years, and approximate collision locations vary across Vancouver roads? The goal is exploratory understanding, not a causal or exposure-adjusted road safety ranking.

Data engineering and geographic matching

  • Normalize street and block identifiers across 2,472,917 input parking-ticket records.
  • Use official road geometry for street-range matching and approximate ICBC collision location assignment.
  • Audit accepted, excluded, unmatched and ambiguous records before generating analysis-ready tables.

Dashboard and interaction

  • Explore parking, collision and comparison analysis layers with multi-year filters.
  • Inspect highlighted road segments, infraction types and road-level change.
  • Select a location and radius to examine nearby collision counts, severity and involvement categories.

Validation and limits

A local end-to-end rebuild passed 37 checks with zero failures, one CDN-related warning and one browser-interactivity check skipped by static QA. Raw ticket and collision counts are not normalized by traffic, parking exposure or enforcement intensity; geographic matches are approximate.

My contribution

Built Python data cleaning and geographic matching for the original group parking analysis and implemented its interactive Folium map. The later ICBC integration and v12-series dashboard are subsequent extensions; the project documentation distinguishes the academic team contribution from later development.
